statements.quote: We report the results of seven total experiments that test these predictions, including four experiments in the main text and three in the Supplementary Material. The first preregistered experiment provides an initial test of our predictions in a naturalistic setting where participants are asked to learn about a particular topic by engaging interactively with either Google or ChatGPT, and then to provide advice to a friend based on what they learned from their search. In the second preregistered experiment, we report a more conservative test of our predictions by exposing participants to search results containing the same set of facts, varying only whether it is presented in the format of an LLM summary or a set of linked websites. In the third experiment, we test for the robustness of the effects in a laboratory setting, this time by holding constant the search engine—Google search—and varying whether participants learned about a topic through standard Google search results or Google’s LLM synthesis (“AI Overview”) presented at the top of the standard search results page. Finally, in the fourth experiment, we explore the downstream consequences of these effects by presenting advice written by participants in a prior experiment to an independent set of “recipients”—blind to the original search platform used to learn about the topic—and examining their willingness to adopt the advice. In the Supplementary Material, we report the results of three preregistered replications that, for example, test for the robustness of the basic effects to the inclusion of real-time web links in LLM syntheses and to a search topic that was of high personal relevance.
statements.locator: p. 3, Empirical analysis (preregistrations and supplementary replications)

statements.quote: Per the preregistered criteria, we excluded 32 participants for failing attention checks, resulting in a final sample of 1,104 participants (Mage = 42.40, 53% female). The preregistration for the study is available at https://aspredicted.org/D1G_BRC.
The full survey instrument is reported in the Supplementary Material.
We also note that we conducted two preregistered replications of experiment 1 (reported in the Supplementary Material due to space limitations).

To address this, in the second preregistered experiment, we employed the same basic procedure as in experiment 1, but rather than conducting real online searches, participants engaged in a simulated Google or ChatGPT search.
The preregistration for the study is available at https://aspredicted.org/3rxx-vktc.pdf.
This 291-word synthesis was used as the simulated response in the ChatGPT condition (see Supplementary Material for the full survey stimulus).

To create equivalent results for the Google condition, we submitted the same 291-word summary back to GPT-4o and asked it to create six different article variations that all retained the same set of facts as in the seven suggestions, but with each one written in the style of an article from a different media outlet, such as Better Homes and Gardens, Martha Stewart, and The New York Times (see Supplementary Material for the instructions submitted to GPT-4o and resulting articles). We then used these articles for the simulated results in the Google condition, which took the form of six links to webpages displaying one of the articles (see Supplementary Material for survey instrument).
statements.locator: p. 6, Experiment 2, Methods (prompts, article stimuli, survey instrument)

statements.quote: Finally, the results of the same mediation model estimated in experiment 1 (reported in the Supplementary Material due to space constraints) lend convergent evidence for the theorized process (Fig. 1).

While repeated exposure to the information likely also played a role in the deeper learning observed in the Google condition, an ex post analysis (reported in the Supplementary Material due to space constraints) revealed that the predicted effects were sustained after controlling for the number of websites visited.

Similar to the prior experiments, participants were first told to imagine that they were asked by a friend for advice on a particular subject—here, how to lead a healthier lifestyle—and that they wanted to gather more information on the topic before writing their advice (see the Supplementary Material for the survey instrument).
The preregistration for the study is available at https://aspredicted. org/6py8-ggdn.pdf.
statements.locator: p. 8, Experiment 4, Method (preregistration; PDF annotation gives https://aspredicted.org/6py8-ggdn.pdf)

statements.quote: Finally, in the Supplementary Material, we report the results of a preregistered conceptual replication of experiment 4 (n = 1,258) that confirm the generalizability of these findings.
Results from seven online and lab experiments—including four reported in the main text and three conceptual replications in the Supplementary Material—lent convergent support for our predictions.

The effects were also robust to a range of search topics, from how to plant a vegetable garden (experiments 1 and 2), to how to lead a healthier lifestyle (experiment 3, Supplementary Material), to what one should do as the victim of a financial scam (Supplementary Material).

Participants reported developing shallower knowledge from LLM summaries versus web search links even when the underlying engine (Google) was held constant (experiment 3), even when the facts in the results were held constant and only the presentation format of the results varied (experiment 2), and even when the LLM syntheses were augmented by real-time web links (Supplementary Material).

For the Google condition, we used ngrok (https://ngrok.com/) to enable the Google site running and Google’s Custom Search JSON API (https://developers.google.com/custom-search/v1/over view) to handle search queries.

deposits.notes:
Title: LLM vs. Google. Found through the hyperlinks on supplement pp. 4 and 6, not by repository search. OSF's node metadata says public=false and anonymous=true, but the exact view-only link published in the supplement permits anonymous listing and download without any account or access request. Access is coded public for this published, functioning link; retain its view_only parameter.

The node metadata, OSF storage listing, children listing and all eight folder listings returned HTTP 200. There are no child components, no linked nodes and no wikis; osfstorage is the sole file provider. Complete recursive inventory: 20 files, comprising seven CSVs, eight survey PDFs and five preregistration PDFs. No analysis code, codebook, README, exclusion log or explicit data license was found.

All seven CSVs were downloaded and read entirely in memory, each under 20 MB. rows_checked and columns_checked refer specifically to Experiment 1/data.csv; the complete per-file checks follow below. No CSV contains an explicit respondent/writer ID or an inclusion/exclusion flag. Writer files place condition, one advice text and numerical outcomes in the same row; recipient files preserve each rater's paired source-specific scores in one row. No completely duplicate rows were found. Repeated advice strings within some writer files were retained as distinct records.

For S1-S3, the observed row counts equal the paper's analyzed sample totals, and means of cosine_similarity, edit_distance and num_unique_entities reproduce the printed arm means to their reported precision. Those score columns vary across rows, so the files contain individual records, not repeated arm aggregates. S3 has 125 Google and 125 AI records.

S5 contains 2,402 rows (google=787, gpt=803, link=812), matching the explicit final sample on supplement p. 2. Its wordcount column is present. In S1-S3 and S6 the advice text is available but the paper's LIWC word-count column is absent; a new word-count measure can be computed, while exact LIWC replication requires the original settings/tool.

S6 contains 1,999 rows (google=1,024, gpt=975), whereas supplement p. 6 says the final sample is 1,976. Its exclusion text and reported F-test degrees of freedom also require reconciliation. There is no attention-check or retained-sample flag in the CSV. These are available-record counts, not a confirmed reconstruction of the published analyzed sample; do not silently treat 1,999 or its arm counts as the paper's analyzed counts.

S4 has 1,493 recipient rows. The condition-labeled choice variable gives google=756, gpt=367, similar=370, resolving the direction of the reversed labels printed on main-paper p. 8 in favor of Google. The 0.key column is google and 1.key is gpt throughout the posted file; this sorted/source-labeled layout does not itself verify presentation-order randomization.

S4 lacks source-writer IDs. There are 127 distinct 0.advice strings and 126 distinct 1.advice strings, versus 125 unique texts per arm in the S3 writer file. Exact matches to S3 exist for 1,176/1,493 Google rating rows and 1,271/1,493 GPT rating rows; NFC and whitespace normalization increases these to 1,210 and 1,316, but does not link every rating. Full per-writer recipient summaries require resolving the remaining text discrepancies.

S7 has 1,258 recipient rows, matching supplement p. 9. It contains 396 distinct Google advice texts and 418 distinct GPT advice texts, matching the source text-pool sizes printed there, with choice variable dv: google=509, gpt=417, similar=332. These are sampled mattress-advice texts embedded in recipient records, not a separately deposited original writer-assignment dataset.

Posted cosine/edit-distance values can support descriptive summaries, and the raw texts permit new diversity analyses. The original scoring/aggregation code and its treatment of pair dependence are absent; the presence of one score per row does not establish valid independent-observation SEs for pairwise diversity metrics.

It contains aggregate replication results, surveys, prompts, six researcher-supplied gardening articles, a mediation model and an additional regression table; it contains no participant-level data table or participant advice corpus. Its filename was confirmed in Europe PMC fullTextXML (HTTP 200) and the PMC Open Access S3 prefix listing (HTTP 200), then the listed file was downloaded (HTTP 200). The publisher's paper-linked supplement page returned HTTP 403 with a bot check; no attempt was made to pass it. what_we_could_compute: Per-arm means, SDs, nonmissing counts and ordinary mean SEs for individual-level numerical outcomes in S1-S3 and S5, plus paired recipient-rating summaries for S4 and S7. One record holds the writer's condition, text and scores, or the recipient's paired ratings. S6 summaries can be computed for the posted 1,999 records, but these would not yet reconstruct the paper's analyzed sample.

final.open_items: studies.S3.arms.n_analyzed is supported by 250 participant-level records, with Google=125 and AI=125. Additional observed analyzed-sample arm counts are S1 google=557/gpt=547, S2 google=988/gpt=991 and S5 google=787/gpt=803/link=812; S1-S3 totals match the main paper and S5 matches the supplement.

final.open_items: studies.S1_S3.outcomes.diversity.unit_and_uncertainty can be partly addressed: each writer record has nonconstant cosine_similarity and edit_distance scores, whose arm means match the paper. Raw advice texts permit new pairwise/text diversity measures and participant-resampling analyses that recompute those measures. The original aggregation algorithm and dependence correction remain unverified without code; naive independent-row SEs for these pairwise-derived scores should not be treated as established precision.

final.open_items: studies.S3.outcomes.helpfulness.relative_choice.reported_and_direction can be checked with S4_data.csv: choice=google for 756 recipients, gpt for 367 and similar for 370. Thus the underlying condition-labeled choice data resolve the reversed labels in the printed comparison. Per-writer mean recipient ratings remain incomplete because writer IDs are absent and not all S4 texts match S3 texts, even after whitespace normalization.

final.open_items: studies.S5.participants.n_analyzed and parts of studies.S5_S7.outcomes are supported by the 2,402-row S5 file and the newly retrieved supplement. S5 includes wordcount, n_unique_entities, cosine_similarity, edit_distance and the original advice. S7 provides 1,258 recipient records with paired helpfulness, informativeness, effort, trust, adoption and recommendation ratings, plus source-labeled mattress-advice texts.

final.open_items: studies.S6.participants.n_analyzed remains unresolved because the CSV has 1,999 records but the supplement reports 1,976 and the file has no inclusion/exclusion indicators. Supplement and preregistration identify the two source conditions and financial-scam task; recovering the reported analyzed rows requires clarification or an exclusion key.

Fresh word counts can be computed from the advice in S1-S3 and S6; the published LIWC count column is not deposited there, so exact replication of that outcome is not confirmed. S5 has a deposited wordcount column. The S7 rating data expose the 396 Google and 418 GPT mattress-advice strings but not original writer IDs or a separate source-writer assignment dataset.
notes:
Checked 2026-10-09 to 2026-10-10. Read all 398 lines of the supplied markdown (all 11 main-paper PDF pages, including notes and references). The main PDF contains no appended supplement; the separate 49-page publisher supplement was retrieved from its public PMC archive and its full extracted text was read. Quoted passages were taken from the PDF text with layout whitespace and soft-hyphen line wrapping normalized; link destinations were recovered from PDF annotations. Some survey pages contain images, so text extraction does not expose all pictured survey items. The supplied form's data_and_code contains only data_url=null and code_url=null.

The decisive deposit is the view-only OSF URL embedded in the publicly available supplement. All seven CSVs were read without login. The status is high-confidence public participant data because multiple writer studies contain observed condition labels, individual scores and advice texts. It does not certify that all published analyses can be exactly reproduced: there is no analysis code, no explicit data license, no retained-sample flag, and S6 and some S4-to-S3 text links need reconciliation.

Deposits count includes one OSF project, one archived supplementary PDF, one GitHub materials repository and five preregistration records. The preregistration PDFs are also copied in OSF; these entries do not represent additional independent participant datasets.

Search details: the required DataCite, Zenodo, Harvard Dataverse and OSF title/first-author searches all ultimately returned HTTP 200. DataCite's author search returned 42 records, Zenodo's author search 7, and all titles/authors were inspected; none was this paper's data. The exact-title searches and Harvard author search returned zero. OSF filter[title]=Melumad searches a title string, not authors; a separate users lookup found Shiri Melumad (f2hdx), whose three public projects were unrelated. A coauthor lookup found Jin Ho Yun (tkuw6); no claim is made to have enumerated that profile's projects. The additional broad OSF LLM (1,235), OSF Google (297) and DataCite 'depth of learning' (105) searches inspected only the first 100 records each; their empty relevant lists are not exhaustive negative findings. The target node has public=false and is not discoverable in these public-title searches. Zenodo initially rejected size=100 with HTTP 400; anonymous size=25 retries succeeded. No additional relevant deposit was confirmed through these searches. The publisher landing-page n_results is null because access stopped at HTTP 403, not a zero-result search.

All network requests used Python urllib and User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1; no personal identifier was sent. No login, account creation, access request or bot-check bypass was attempted. Data and supplementary files were inspected only in memory. The only intended filesystem write is forms/data/c489.json.
